title: Why am I applying for jobs but getting no interviews?
metaTitle: Why am I applying for jobs but getting no interviews?
metaDescription: You've updated your CV and kept applying. Still nothing. Let's check where your search might be getting stuck and what you can try next.

sections.heading: Start here
body: You've changed your CV. You've uploaded it again. You've filled in an application form that asks for everything already on your CV. Then you check your inbox, and there's nothing.
After a while, the silence starts to feel personal. You begin wondering whether your experience counts for anything.

Before you rewrite the whole document again, let's look at where your search might be getting stuck. Your CV matters, but it is one part of a process you don't fully control. The role you're choosing, the evidence you give and the way you apply all deserve a closer look.
You can do this check with one recent application. Open the advert beside the CV you sent. That's where we'll start.

sections.heading: Are you applying for work you can explain your fit for?
body: When you need a job, being told to narrow your search can sound ridiculous. Of course you're open to different things. You have bills.
You can keep more than one option open. What helps is giving each option a clear reason to consider you.

For each advert, write down the main things the person will need to do. Look beyond the title. Two jobs called "administrator" can involve very different work: one might centre on diaries and correspondence, another on stock records and supplier follow-ups.

Next to each requirement, write a real example of when you've done something similar. If the advert asks for a specific licence or qualification, check whether it is essential. A willingness to learn won't replace every entry requirement.

You don't have to match every preference. You do need to explain why the work is within reach. If that explanation is difficult, pause before spending another hour on the application. You may need a different role, a clearer example or some experience you haven't built yet.

sections.heading: Does your CV show the work, or only name it?
body: "Responsible for administration" might be accurate. It also leaves someone guessing what you actually handled.
Here's an illustrative rewrite: "Maintained stock records, followed up missing delivery documents and prepared the weekly order summary for the supervisor."
That gives a reader something to picture. It doesn't need a dramatic percentage or an award to be useful. Only use details you can stand behind.
Read the first half-page of your CV. Would a stranger understand the work you want and the experience that supports it? Or would they need to piece your story together from five different jobs?

Put the most relevant evidence where it's easy to find. Keep your real job titles, but explain the responsibilities that connect to the vacancy. Use the employer's terms when they accurately describe your experience. Don't add a skill simply because it appears in the advert.

If you're worried about the file itself, the [ATS CV guide](/insights/ats-cv-south-africa-4-minute-fix) covers formatting checks. An ATS is the software some employers use to manage applications. Passing a formatting check doesn't guarantee an interview, but it can help you catch avoidable problems.

sections.heading: Check the boring things before changing everything
body: Open the exact file you submitted. Is it the right version? Does it open properly? Are your phone number and email address correct? Did the application ask for a document you forgot to attach?

Check your voicemail and spam folder too. If someone calls during work hours, have a short response ready: "Thanks for calling. I'm unable to speak privately right now. Could we arrange a time later today?"
These details won't solve a difficult job market. They are worth checking because they're fixable, and they're easy to miss when you're tired.

sections.heading: Where are you looking?
body: If every application comes through one app, try adding a second route that suits your field. That could be an employer's own careers page, a relevant recruitment agency or a conversation with a former colleague.

When a vacancy appears on a job board, check the employer's official application instructions. Use the stated route. Sending the same application to every address you can find may create confusion rather than help.

You can also make it easier for people to understand what you're looking for. "Please let me know if you hear of anything" gives them very little to work with. "I'm looking for office support roles where I can use my scheduling and supplier coordination experience" is easier to remember.
Your [LinkedIn profile](/insights/linkedin-profile-optimisation-south-africa-2026) can support that message. It should tell the same basic story as your application.

sections.heading: Keep a record that helps you make decisions
body: You don't need a complicated spreadsheet. A notebook is enough. For each application, record the role, employer, date, CV version and how far you got. Add a short note about why the role suited you.

After a few weeks, look for patterns. Are you getting calls for one type of role but silence for another? Are you reaching interviews, then going no further? Those are different problems and need different work.
Use this small worksheet for your next application:

items: The main work in this role is...
The requirement I'm least clear about is...
The change I'll make before applying is...
The response or next step was...

body: There isn't a universal number of applications you should send before an interview arrives. Comparing your search with a stranger's total can make a hard week worse without telling you what to change.

sections.heading: What if you've done all of this?
body: Then it may be time for another pair of eyes. Ask someone to compare one advert with your application and tell you where your fit becomes unclear. A specific question will usually help more than "Is my CV okay?"

There will also be things you can't see: another candidate's experience, an internal decision, a changed budget or a paused vacancy. Silence doesn't tell you which of those happened. It certainly doesn't tell you your worth.
Choose one useful change for your next few applications and keep a record of what happens. That gives you something to learn from, even when the process feels frustratingly quiet.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the CV itself, a [CV Revamp](/buy/cv-revamp) starts with the role you're targeting. If you'd rather talk through the whole search first, [book a free discovery call](/book/discovery). Bring a vacancy and the CV you used, and we can start with the actual application in front of us.

title: How to ask for a promotion when you're already doing more than your job
metaTitle: How to ask for a promotion when you're already doing more than your job
metaDescription: The extra responsibility is already yours. Here's how to prepare a clear conversation about the role, recognition and next steps you're asking for.

sections.heading: Start here
body: You're the person people call when something goes wrong. You help the new starters. You cover for your manager. Somehow, extra responsibility keeps finding you.
But when you think about asking for a promotion, you hesitate. What if they say you're getting ahead of yourself? What if they remind you that everyone is working hard?

It can feel uncomfortable to put your own name forward, especially when you've built a reputation for being reliable and easy to work with. Still, your manager may not know what you want next. They may see the help you're giving without recognising how much your role has changed.
You can make that change easier to see. Start by getting clear about the role you want, then prepare a conversation about the work you've been doing and what would need to happen next.

sections.heading: Name the move you're asking for
body: "I'd like to grow" leaves a lot open to interpretation. You might mean a better salary. Your manager might hear that you'd enjoy a training course.
Are you asking for a team leader position? A more senior role in the work you already do? A formal change to responsibilities you've been carrying for months?

A promotion and a salary review can be connected, but they aren't always the same conversation. If you want both, say so clearly. If there isn't a suitable next role in your organisation, you may first need a discussion about what progression could realistically look like.
Try writing one sentence before you book the meeting: "I'd like to discuss moving into ___ because my current work now includes ___."

If you can't finish it yet, find out more about the next role. Ask for the job description or speak to someone who understands its responsibilities. Being excellent in your current job matters. The next job may ask something different of you.

sections.heading: Build a case you can fit on one page
body: You don't need a presentation with twenty slides. You need a few examples that make the change in your work clear.
For each example, describe what needed attention, what you personally did and what happened afterwards. Include the people who can confirm it or the work records that support it.

Here's an illustrative example. "I help the team" becomes: "When two new colleagues joined, I prepared a handover guide, walked them through the weekly reporting process and became their first contact for questions. The supervisor then used that guide for the next starter."
The second version explains the contribution. It doesn't pretend you managed a whole department. It also doesn't invent a number to sound impressive.

Choose examples that relate to the role you want. If you're asking to lead a team, include evidence of how you help others deliver, deal with problems and take responsibility for decisions. Working the longest hours isn't enough to explain readiness for management.

Your page can have four short sections: the role you're asking about, the relevant work you've done, the responsibilities you're ready to take on and any development you still need. You can acknowledge a gap without talking yourself out of the conversation.

sections.heading: Ask for a proper meeting
body: A quick comment while your manager is leaving for another appointment probably won't get the attention this deserves.

You could write: "I'd like to set aside time to discuss my progression and the responsibilities I've taken on. I'm interested in the team leader role and would like your feedback on my readiness and the process for being considered. Would we be able to book half an hour?"
Use the actual role and the language that feels natural to you. You're asking for a work conversation, not a favour.

If your organisation has a review or promotion cycle, find out when decisions are prepared, who is involved and what information they need. The date of your performance review may be later than the date the budget was discussed.

sections.heading: Say what you want, then leave room for an answer
body: In the meeting, make your request early. You don't need to spend fifteen minutes proving that you're grateful before you're allowed to talk about progression.

"I'd like to be considered for the team leader role. Over the past few months I've taken responsibility for these parts of the team's work. I'd like to understand how you assess my readiness and what the next steps would be."
Talk through your strongest examples. Then listen. Your manager may raise something you hadn't considered, such as a responsibility you haven't yet had a chance to demonstrate.
Ask for specifics. "What would good performance in that area look like?" is more useful than leaving with "I need to be more strategic" and no idea what that means on Monday morning.

sections.heading: If the answer is "not yet"
body: Find out what "yet" depends on. Is there a skill to develop? Does a role need to become available? Is there a formal assessment or application process?
You can say: "I'd like to work on the gap you've identified. Can we agree on an opportunity to demonstrate it and a date to review the progress?"
Make sure the opportunity is realistic alongside your workload. Taking on unlimited extra work with no clear criteria can leave you exhausted and no closer to a decision.

If the answer is "no budget", ask whether your readiness and the funding decision are separate issues. You might agree on development work, a future review or a different responsibility. None of those is a confirmed promotion. Keep the distinction clear for yourself.

sections.heading: Write down what was agreed
body: Send a short follow-up: "Thank you for the conversation. My understanding is that I'll work on ___, with support from ___. We'll review this on ___. The decision about ___ is still outstanding. Please let me know if I've missed anything."

If a promotion is offered, clarify the title, responsibilities, pay and effective date through the employer's formal process. Enthusiasm in a meeting is encouraging; you still need to understand the actual offer.

And if the conversation stays vague after repeated attempts? That's information you can use when planning your next move. You don't have to make a rushed decision, but you can start comparing your options with clearer eyes.

The [career-planning guide](/insights/career-planning-when-you-feel-stuck-south-africa) can help with that reflection. If you want to prepare for your own conversation, a [free discovery call](/book/discovery) gives us space to work through the words and the evidence together.

title: How to network for a job when you don't know anyone in your industry
metaTitle: How to network for a job when you don't know anyone in your industry
metaDescription: Start with one person and a question you genuinely want answered. Practical messages and follow-ups for building professional connections without the awkward pitch.

sections.heading: Start here
body: "You need to network."

People say it as though there is a room somewhere where useful contacts are waiting for you to arrive. Meanwhile, you're trying to work out who to message and how to avoid sounding as though you're asking a stranger to solve your life.

If networking feels awkward, start smaller. You can ask a thoughtful question, reconnect with someone you already know or join a conversation about work that interests you. You don't need a large circle before you can begin.

The first aim is to understand the work and build a relationship that both people are comfortable with. A job lead may come from that. It may not. The conversation can still help you make a better decision.

sections.heading: Be clear enough for someone to help
body: "I'm looking for anything" is an honest description of how desperate a job search can feel. It's also difficult for another person to act on.
Give them a starting point: the kind of work you're exploring, the experience you bring and the question you have.
For example: "I'm looking into office support roles. I've handled scheduling and customer queries, and I'd like to understand what employers expect from junior administrators."

That doesn't lock you into one career forever. It makes this particular conversation easier. If you're exploring several directions, have a clear question for each rather than asking one person to advise on everything.

Your [LinkedIn profile](/insights/linkedin-profile-optimisation-south-africa-2026) can back up the message. When someone looks you up, they should be able to understand the experience you're referring to.

sections.heading: Begin closer to home than you think
body: Make a short list of people you've studied with, worked with, volunteered alongside or met through a professional event. You may not have spoken for a while. That's okay; acknowledge it naturally.

You can also look for alumni groups, professional associations and public events relevant to your interests. Check whether there is a free or online option before committing money or travel time. You don't need to buy access to an expensive conference to have a useful conversation.
Choose people because there is a sensible connection to your question. A person doing the work you want to understand may be more useful than the most senior person you can find.

sections.heading: Send a message that is easy to answer
body: The examples below are fictional messages you can adapt. Replace the details with your own and write in a way you'd actually speak.

To a former colleague: "Hi Lerato, it's been a while. I hope you're well. I'm exploring coordinator roles and remembered that you moved into operations. Would you be comfortable telling me which skills helped you make that move? I'm trying to understand what I should work on next."

To someone from your college or university: "Hi Thabo, I noticed we both studied at the same institution. I've recently completed my qualification and I'm exploring office support roles. If you have a moment, I'd appreciate your view on one thing: what do new starters often underestimate about the work?"

To someone whose public work you've followed: "Hi Ayesha, your post about training new staff caught my attention. I'm in customer support and have been helping colleagues learn our system. I'm considering training coordination. Would you be open to one or two questions about the day-to-day work? No problem if you're unable to."
Each message explains the connection and makes a small request. There is no need for a long introduction, flattery or an unexpected CV attachment.

sections.heading: If they say yes, respect the time they've offered
body: Prepare a few questions you couldn't easily answer by reading their profile. Ask what the work involves, how people usually enter the field or which skill would be useful to practise first.
If you agree on a fifteen-minute call, keep an eye on the time. You can say, "We're nearly at the time we agreed. May I ask one last question?" Let them decide whether to continue.
Listen closely enough to ask a follow-up about what they've said. You don't have to work through a script of questions if the conversation has already answered them.
Avoid asking for confidential details about their employer, applicants or colleagues. You can learn a lot about a field without putting someone in an uncomfortable position.

sections.heading: When is it okay to ask about opportunities?
body: If there is a specific vacancy and the conversation makes it appropriate, you can ask about the application process: "I noticed the coordinator vacancy on your company's careers page. Do you know whether applications should go directly through that page?"
A referral is a bigger request. The person may not know your work well enough to recommend you, or their employer may have a particular process. Give them an easy way to say no.
"If you feel you know my work well enough, would you be comfortable referring me? I understand if you'd prefer that I apply directly."
Apply through the required route either way. A conversation doesn't replace the employer's process, and knowing someone doesn't guarantee an interview.

sections.heading: Follow up without chasing
body: If an initial message gets no reply, one brief follow-up after a week or two is a reasonable personal approach. You could say, "Just following up on my message in case it got buried. I understand if now isn't a good time."
Then leave it there. People may be busy, away or unable to help. Repeated messages can turn a small request into pressure.
After a useful conversation, send a specific thank-you. "Your explanation of the reporting work helped me understand what I need to practise" means more than a copied paragraph of praise.

If you later use their advice, a short update can keep the relationship going naturally. You can also share something useful when it fits, but you don't need to manufacture a favour to repay them immediately.

sections.heading: Make room for this in your actual week
body: Try a small routine you can sustain: choose one person, read enough to make a relevant approach and send a thoughtful message. Keep a note of any reply and the next step you agreed on.

Continue applying for suitable roles. Networking is another route to information and relationships, not a reason to stop the rest of your search. If applications are going quiet, the [job-search check](/insights/applying-for-jobs-no-interviews-south-africa) can help you review that part too.

If you want your profile to explain the direction you're moving in before people look you up, [LinkedIn Optimisation](/buy/linkedin) is built for that. For your first message, though, keep it simple. Choose one person and one question you genuinely want to understand.

title: Changing careers at 30, 35 or 40: how to test a move before you leave
metaTitle: Changing careers at 30, 35 or 40: how to test a move before you leave
metaDescription: You want different work, but you have a life to support. Explore your options, understand what transfers and test a direction before making a big move.

sections.heading: Start here
body: You can be grateful for your job and still wonder how long you can keep doing it.

Maybe you've stopped learning. Maybe the work has never felt right, but there was always a reason to stay. Now you're looking at another career and thinking about the years you've already invested in this one.
Then come the practical questions. Would you need another qualification? Could you afford a lower salary? Would anyone take your experience seriously in a different field?
Those questions deserve more than "It's never too late". You need enough information to decide what kind of change makes sense for your life. You can begin collecting it while you're still employed.

sections.heading: Work out what you actually want to change
body: Before choosing a new career, separate the work from the circumstances around it.

Would you enjoy the same role with a different manager? Is the commute taking more out of you than the work itself? Are you interested in a different kind of work, or do you mainly need more responsibility and better pay?

Write down what you want less of and what you want more of. Be specific. "I want to be happy" is understandable, but it won't help you compare two roles. "I want more time solving problems and less time making repetitive calls" gives you something to investigate.

You may discover that a move within your organisation would help. You may realise the whole field is wrong for you. Either answer is useful. The [career-planning guide](/insights/career-planning-when-you-feel-stuck-south-africa) can help if you're still trying to name what's bothering you.

sections.heading: Take your experience apart before you dismiss it
body: It's easy to reduce ten years of work to a job title. Look at the tasks underneath it.

Perhaps you've handled difficult customers, trained new starters, kept records accurate or coordinated people who had different priorities. Those skills may be useful elsewhere, although a new role could still require specialist knowledge or a formal qualification.

Here's an illustrative example. Someone in customer support wants to explore training coordination. They have helped colleagues learn a new system and written instructions that the team uses. Those experiences give them a starting point. They still need to find out whether target roles involve organising training, designing learning material, facilitating sessions or all of those things.

Write down a skill, the example that proves it and a role where it might be useful. Keep your original job title honest. You can explain relevant work without relabelling yourself as someone you've never been.

sections.heading: What changes at 30, 35 or 40?
body: Your age doesn't decide whether a change is possible. It does change what the move costs and what you bring to it.

At 30, you may still have room to study part-time, take a junior role or try something for a year and change your mind. You also have fewer years of evidence to point to, so a practical project can carry more weight.

By 35 or 40, there's often more relying on your income: a bond, school fees, family members you support. You also bring more experience of handling people, pressure and responsibility. That makes adjacent roles worth a serious look. A move that uses half of what you already know may get you there with less of a pay drop than starting from the bottom.

An employer may wonder whether someone with your experience will settle into a more junior role. Answer that directly in your application. Explain why you're choosing the move and how you'll handle being the newer person in the room.

sections.heading: Check what the new work is like on an ordinary Tuesday
body: A job can look appealing from a distance. Before committing to it, find out what people actually spend their time doing.
Read several recent adverts for the same kind of role. Note the repeated tasks, entry requirements and tools. Separate requirements that appear consistently from an unusual wish list in one advert.

Speak to someone doing the work if you can. Ask what takes up most of their week, what newcomers underestimate and how people usually enter the field. "What do you find frustrating about the work?" may tell you more than asking whether they enjoy it.

You don't have to ask for a job. A short, respectful request for information is enough: "I'm exploring a move from customer support into training coordination. Would you be open to answering two questions about the day-to-day work? I understand if you're unable to."
One person's experience won't describe every workplace. Compare what they tell you with adverts and other conversations.

sections.heading: Try a small version of the work
body: Look for a way to test the activity before paying for a long course or leaving your role. You might shadow someone with permission, take on a relevant internal project or complete a small practice task using fictional information.
For the training example, that could mean preparing a short guide and asking someone to use it. Did you enjoy explaining the process? Could they follow it? What needed changing?

Respect your current responsibilities and any restrictions on outside work. Don't use confidential employer or customer information in a practice project or portfolio. A fictional example can still demonstrate your thinking.

Keep the experiment small enough to finish. You are trying to learn whether the work suits you and what you need to develop. A half-finished collection of courses may tell you less than one completed piece of work and useful feedback.

sections.heading: Put the practical constraints on paper
body: If other people rely on your income, that matters. So do transport, study time, care responsibilities and the cost of any required qualification.

Find out what entry into the new role could involve. Can you make an internal move? Are there adjacent roles that use more of your existing experience? Would you be starting at a lower level, and is that manageable for your household?

Write down the costs you can identify and the questions you still need answered. Avoid building the plan around a salary you've seen once online or an assumption that work will follow immediately after a course.

If the move depends on a professional registration or qualification, confirm the requirements with the relevant official body before enrolling. A short course can be useful, but it won't substitute for every formal entry route.

sections.heading: Give yourself a month to learn something concrete
body: During the first week, choose one possible direction and collect a small set of relevant adverts. In the second, speak to people who understand the work. Use the third week for a practical task or an introductory learning activity. In the fourth, review what you've found.
Ask yourself: Do I still want the work now that I understand it better? Which parts of my experience transfer? What is the smallest sensible next step? What would make me pause?
You might decide to continue, explore an adjacent role or leave this option alone. None of those outcomes means the month was wasted. You have information you didn't have before.

sections.heading: Explain the move as a considered choice
body: When you start applying, connect your existing experience to the new role. "I need a change" explains your feeling. The employer also needs to understand what you can contribute.

You could say: "My customer support work included helping new colleagues learn our systems. That led me to explore training coordination. I've since completed a small learning project and spoken with people in the field, and I'd like to build on that experience in this role."
Adapt that example to what you've actually done. You don't need to apologise for having a career before this one.

If you want help comparing your options, a [Career Clarity Session](/book/clarity) can give the decision some structure. For now, choose one role to investigate. You can take the question seriously without making your whole life change this week.

title: How to prepare for a job interview using the experience you already have
metaTitle: How to prepare for a job interview using the experience you already have
metaDescription: You don't need forty perfect answers. Prepare real examples, practise saying them aloud and arrive knowing what you want to ask too.

sections.heading: Start here
body: The interview invitation arrives and, for a moment, you're relieved. Someone wants to speak to you.

Then you start preparing. You find a list of common questions, open another tab, watch a video and suddenly have forty possible answers to remember. By the time someone asks you to describe yourself, you've forgotten how you normally speak.
Let's make this more manageable. Start with the job and a few real examples from your experience. You'll have something solid to talk about even when the question comes in a form you didn't expect.
You don't need to become a different person for the interview. You do need to make your experience understandable to someone who wasn't there.

sections.heading: Read the advert as a description of someone's working day
body: Go back to the job description. What will this person be expected to handle? Perhaps they'll deal with customer complaints, organise deliveries, check records or coordinate a small team.
Choose the responsibilities that seem central to the role. For each one, ask yourself: "When have I done this, or something close to it?"

An employer asking for "attention to detail" might need someone who catches mistakes before an order goes out. Saying you're detail-oriented doesn't give them much to assess. Describing how you spotted a mismatch, checked it and corrected the order does.

Make a simple note with two columns: "What the role needs" and "An example I can discuss". If one requirement has no example beside it, think about what you do know and how you'd explain the gap honestly. Don't create experience to fill the space.

sections.heading: Choose stories you remember clearly
body: Think of a time you solved a problem, worked through a disagreement, learned something unfamiliar or corrected a mistake. Choose examples where you can explain your own part.

If you're early in your career, your examples may come from a group assignment, volunteering, part-time work or helping in a family business. Say where the experience came from. It can demonstrate a useful skill without being presented as a full-time job.
You might have heard of STAR. It stands for situation, task, action and result. In ordinary language: what was happening, what needed doing, what you did and how it turned out.
Use that structure to keep yourself on track. You don't need to announce each letter or make every answer sound like it came out of a textbook.

sections.heading: Give your actions enough space
body: Here's an illustrative example for a customer support interview:

"A customer contacted us because a delivery hadn't arrived when expected. I checked the order record and found that the address had been captured incorrectly. I confirmed the details with the customer, contacted dispatch and agreed on a new delivery time. I then called the customer back with the update. The order was delivered, and I flagged the capture error to my supervisor so we could check how it had happened."
That answer gives the interviewer something to ask about. How did you handle the customer's frustration? What did you do while waiting for dispatch? What would you change next time?

Notice that the example doesn't end with a made-up satisfaction score. A result can be an issue resolved, a deadline met or a mistake caught. If you have reliable numbers, use them. If you don't, explain the outcome you actually know.
When reviewing your own answers, check how much time you spend describing the background. A short explanation is usually enough. Leave room for the decisions you made and the actions you took.

sections.heading: Practise speaking, not only writing
body: An answer that looks clear on a page can become a very long story out loud. Record yourself answering one question on your phone. Listen once, without picking apart every pause.
Could someone follow what happened? Did you explain your contribution? Did you answer the question? Choose one thing to improve and try again.

Keep brief notes rather than memorising a script. You want to remember the example well enough to adapt it. If the interviewer asks about teamwork, you'll explain how you worked with others. If they ask about a mistake, you may use the same experience but focus on what went wrong and how you responded.

If you lose your place in the interview, you can pause: "Let me give you a clearer example." You can also ask them to repeat or clarify a question. A short pause gives you a chance to answer the question they actually asked.

sections.heading: Prepare an opening and a few questions of your own
body: For "Tell me about yourself", practise a brief introduction that connects your current experience to the role. Give them a useful starting point, then let the conversation develop. You don't need your entire life story in the first answer.

Read the employer's official website and the information they've sent you. Look for what the organisation does, who it serves and where this job fits. You don't need to pretend you've admired the company since childhood.

Prepare questions you genuinely want answered. "What would you want the person in this role to have achieved after three months?" can help you understand expectations. "What is the biggest challenge the team is dealing with?" may tell you something the advert doesn't.
If salary comes up, be clear about the basis of any figure you discuss and ask what the package includes. It's reasonable to need details before you can compare an opportunity properly.

sections.heading: Sort out the practical details early
body: Confirm the time, location and format. For an in-person interview, check the route and allow for transport delays. Keep the contact person's details somewhere you can find them quickly.

For a video interview, test the link, microphone and camera. Charge your device and think about what you'll do if your connection drops. If data or a private space is a problem, raise it early and ask what options are available.
Have your CV, the advert and a few brief notes nearby. If you plan to take notes during the conversation, say so. Keep confidential material from previous employers out of any work samples you share.

sections.heading: If the interview is tomorrow
body: You can still prepare usefully. Read the advert, choose a few relevant examples and say your opening answer out loud. Check the employer's website, prepare two questions and confirm the logistics. Then give yourself time to rest.

Afterwards, make a quick note of the questions you found difficult and the next steps you were given. If the stated response date passes, a polite follow-up is reasonable. An unanswered message doesn't tell you exactly what happened inside the organisation.
For now, pick one experience and practise explaining it clearly. That's a much better starting point than trying to memorise forty perfect answers.

If you'd like support preparing for a particular role, [book a free discovery call](/book/discovery). We can use your own examples and the actual job description, so the practice feels relevant to the conversation you're about to have.

dek: A clear opening answer helps the interviewer understand your experience. Build yours with examples for graduates, experienced candidates and career changers.
imageAlt: Man in a navy jacket speaking to an interviewer across an office table
title: "Tell me about yourself": how to build a clear interview answer
metaTitle: "Tell me about yourself": how to build a clear interview answer
metaDescription: A clear opening answer helps the interviewer understand your experience. Build yours with examples for graduates, experienced candidates and career changers.

sections.heading: Start here
body: You know yourself. You've been yourself your whole life. So why does this question suddenly make you forget everything you've ever done?
Part of the difficulty is how open it sounds. Are they asking about your qualifications? Your current job? Where you grew up? Should you start at the beginning?
For a job interview, give the person a short introduction to the experience that's relevant to the role. Think of it as helping them know where to begin the conversation with you.
You don't need to squeeze every achievement into the opening answer. Choose the details that make the next question easier to ask.

sections.heading: Start with the work that's relevant now
body: Begin with a plain description of what you do or what you've been preparing to do. If you're between jobs, you can describe your experience without pretending you're currently employed.
"I have four years of experience in office support, mostly handling schedules, records and supplier follow-ups" gives someone a clear starting point.

Then add a relevant example or area of responsibility. Finish by connecting that experience to the opportunity in front of you. This gives your answer a direction instead of turning it into a spoken version of every line on your CV.
Around a minute is a useful practice starting point, but it isn't a rule for every interview. Follow any time limit you're given, and watch for the interviewer wanting to move into questions.

sections.heading: If you're applying for your first professional role
body: The following is an illustrative example. The person and experience are invented for teaching purposes; use only details that are true for you.

"I've recently completed a diploma in business management, and I'm looking for an opportunity in office administration. During my final-year group project, I kept track of deadlines, organised our shared documents and followed up with the team when information was missing. I enjoyed the coordination side of the work. This role interests me because I'd be able to use those skills while learning how your team manages its day-to-day operations."
The answer names the qualification and explains an example. It also makes the limits of the experience clear. A student project is described as a student project.

You can draw on volunteering, part-time work or responsibilities in a community group too. Choose an example that relates to the advertised work. You don't need to begin with an apology about having "no experience" if you have something useful to discuss.

sections.heading: If you've been working for several years
body: Here's another fictional example:

"I'm an office administrator with five years of experience supporting a busy operations team. My work includes coordinating diaries, keeping supplier documents up to date and preparing information for weekly meetings. More recently, I've been helping new colleagues learn those processes, which I've enjoyed. I'm interested in this senior administrator role because it would let me take on more responsibility for how the office runs."
This person doesn't list all five years month by month. They select responsibilities that explain their fit and give a reason for the next step.

If your strongest example includes an outcome you can verify, add it. You don't need to force a number into the answer. "The guide I wrote is now used to train new starters" says something useful on its own, provided it's true.

sections.heading: If you're changing direction
body: A career change can make the question feel harder because you want to explain the move without spending the whole answer defending it.
Try a connection between your existing work and the direction you've researched. This example is also fictional:

"My background is in customer support, where I've spent several years helping people solve problems with orders and services. Part of that work involved explaining our systems to new colleagues. I became interested in training coordination through that experience, so I've been exploring the role and have completed a small practice project organising a training session. I'm interested in this position because it combines coordination with helping people learn, and I can bring practical experience of the questions staff face when using a system."
The answer explains the connection. It doesn't claim that customer support and training coordination are identical, or that a practice project replaces years of specialist experience.

If you're still unsure how to explain your move, work through the [career-change guide](/insights/career-change-south-africa-before-you-leave) before polishing the wording. Sometimes the sentence is difficult because the decision itself needs more thought.

sections.heading: Choose what to leave out
body: You can share personal information when it feels relevant and comfortable. You don't need to provide your family history, private circumstances or every reason you've ever left a job in this opening answer.

If you've had a difficult experience with a previous employer, prepare a separate, measured answer for questions about leaving. Opening with the whole dispute can use up the time you need to explain what you bring to this role.

Also check for descriptions that anyone could use: "hardworking", "passionate", "a people's person". You may be all of those things. A short example helps the interviewer understand what those words mean in your working life.

sections.heading: Write notes you can speak from
body: Take a page and complete these prompts:

items: The experience I want them to understand first is...
One example that connects to this role is...
I'm interested in this opportunity because...

body: Say the answer aloud, then stop looking at the page and try again in your own words. If the wording changes but the meaning stays clear, that's fine. You're practising a conversation.

Record yourself once. Listen for parts where you get lost in background detail or make a claim without explaining it. Cut one unnecessary sentence and try again. You don't need to remove every pause or sound like a presenter.

If you go blank in the interview, take a breath and start with the plainest true sentence: "My background is in..." You can ask for a moment to gather your thoughts. An imperfect opening doesn't prevent you from giving useful answers afterwards.

sections.heading: Prepare for the question that comes next
body: Anything you mention may lead to a follow-up. If you say you improved a process, be ready to explain what changed and what you personally did. If you mention a project, know enough about it to talk beyond the polished opening.

The [interview preparation guide](/insights/interview-preparation-south-africa) will help you build those examples. If you'd like to practise with someone, [book a free discovery call](/book/discovery).
For now, start with the experience you want this employer to understand. You already know the story. The work is choosing where to begin.

dek: The salary question doesn't have to become a guessing game. Prepare a researched range, understand the package and find words you're comfortable saying.
imageAlt: Hands writing in a notebook beside a calculator and two comparison documents
title: What are your salary expectations? How to answer in a South African interview
metaTitle: What are your salary expectations? How to answer in a South African interview
metaDescription: The salary question doesn't have to become a guessing game. Prepare a researched range, understand the package and find words you're comfortable saying.

sections.heading: Start here
body: The conversation is going well. You've explained your experience, asked a thoughtful question and started imagining yourself in the role.
Then someone asks what you'd like to earn.
Suddenly you're trying to calculate your value, your monthly expenses and the risk of saying the wrong thing, all while looking perfectly relaxed on a video call.

You can prepare for this part too. You need a researched range, a clear understanding of what the numbers mean and a few words you feel comfortable saying. You don't need to guess the one magical figure that makes an employer say yes.

sections.heading: Make sure you're discussing the same kind of number
body: Before comparing figures, clarify whether you're talking about monthly or annual pay, and whether the figure is gross salary or cost to company.

Gross pay is pay before deductions. Net pay is what remains after deductions. Cost to company, usually shortened to CTC, describes the employer's total package cost and may include contributions or benefits that won't arrive as cash in your account. The exact breakdown matters.
You can simply ask: "Is that figure monthly CTC, and could you talk me through what's included?"

There's no embarrassment in checking. Comparing your current take-home pay with a proposed CTC figure can make an offer look better than it is. If a term on a payslip or offer letter is unfamiliar, ask HR what it means before you compare figures.

sections.heading: Research the role you're moving into
body: Look at recent adverts with salary ranges for comparable work. Match the responsibilities, experience level and location as closely as you can. A familiar title doesn't always mean a similar job.

Published salary guides can help you establish a starting point. Large job boards and specialist recruiters publish salary guides from time to time, often for a particular field. Check when the information was collected and whether the figures are monthly, annual, gross or CTC.

Keep a few notes: the source, its date, the kind of role and the stated range. If your research produces very different figures, investigate why. You may be comparing different levels of responsibility or very different packages.

Your current salary is one piece of information. The scope of the new role also matters, particularly if you've been underpaid or are taking on significantly different work. Avoid building your whole expectation around a fixed percentage increase.

sections.heading: Decide what would work for you before the call
body: Privately, work out what you need to understand before accepting an offer. That includes the package itself and costs that may change, such as transport or childcare.

Keep your preferred range separate from the lowest offer you could realistically accept. You don't have to volunteer your minimum at the start of the conversation. And don't give a range whose lower end you already know won't work for you.

The figure you discuss with the employer should have a reason behind it: the role, your relevant experience and the evidence you've gathered. Your household costs matter to your decision, but the employer will also be assessing the position's budget and responsibilities.

sections.heading: If they ask before you've heard enough about the role
body: Try: "I'd like to understand the responsibilities and package a little better before giving you a firm expectation. Could you share the range budgeted for the role?"

They may share it. They may ask you to give your expectation first. If you've done the research, you can give a range and explain what it's based on, while making clear that the full package still needs discussion.
You don't need to turn the conversation into a battle over who says a number first. Your aim is to find out whether the opportunity could work for both sides.

sections.heading: If you're ready to give a range
body: Here's a fictional example of the wording, not a salary recommendation: "Based on the responsibilities we've discussed and the comparable roles I've researched, I'm looking at R30,000 to R34,000 monthly CTC. I'd like to understand the benefits and how the package is structured before making a final decision."
Use figures supported by your own research. Be prepared to explain the experience you bring, especially if you're asking for the upper end of the employer's range.

If they ask about your current package and you choose to discuss it, describe it accurately. Don't inflate a figure or invent benefits to strengthen your position. You can still explain why your expectation for the new role differs.

sections.heading: Compare the whole offer
body: Imagine two fictional offers, each described as R30,000 monthly CTC. One includes R3,000 in employer retirement contributions within that total. The other has a different benefits structure. Those headline figures don't tell you what your gross cash pay or take-home pay would be.

Ask for a written breakdown. Check what is guaranteed, what depends on performance and which contributions sit inside the quoted total. A possible bonus shouldn't quietly become part of your guaranteed monthly budget.
Write down these questions for each offer:

items: What is the guaranteed gross cash pay?
Which benefits and employer contributions are included in the CTC figure?
What deductions would apply to me?
Is any commission or bonus guaranteed, and what are its conditions?
What extra costs would I take on to do the job?

body: Ask payroll or HR to clarify the parts you don't understand. An estimated payslip can be helpful, although your actual deductions depend on your circumstances. Don't assume that dividing annual CTC by twelve gives your monthly take-home pay.

sections.heading: If the offer is below what you expected
body: You can be appreciative and still ask a question: "Thank you for the offer. I'm interested in the role. Based on the scope and the experience I'd bring, I was hoping for a package closer to ___. Is there flexibility?"

Give them time to respond. If the salary can't change, ask about other terms that matter to you. Those might include working arrangements, development support or the timing and criteria for a review. A promised future review is not a guaranteed increase, so understand what is actually being offered.
You may decide the offer works for you. You may decide it doesn't. Either way, try to make the decision with the details in writing rather than the excitement or pressure of the call.

For help with the rest of the conversation, read the [interview preparation guide](/insights/interview-preparation-south-africa). If you'd like to practise discussing your experience and expectations, [book a free discovery call](/book/discovery).

dek: Before you pay for another certificate, check what you'll learn, what it costs and how you'll use it. Choose a course that supports the work you want to do.
imageAlt: Man wearing headphones taking notes while following a lesson on his laptop
title: Which short course is worth your time? Start with the job you want
metaTitle: Which short course is worth your time? Start with the job you want
metaDescription: Before you pay for another certificate, check what you'll learn, what it costs and how you'll use it. Choose a course that supports the work you want to do.

sections.heading: Start here
body: You've found a course. The description sounds promising, the certificate looks professional and there's a discount that ends soon.
You're tempted. Doing something feels better than waiting for an opportunity, especially when your job search has been quiet or your career feels stuck.
Before you enrol, ask one question: what do I want to be able to do when I finish?
That question can save you money and weekends. A course may be useful, but "add another certificate to my CV" doesn't tell you whether it's the right one for the work you want.

sections.heading: Choose a role to investigate first
body: You don't need a complete five-year plan. Pick one realistic role or a responsibility you'd like to take on in your current job.

Read several recent adverts for that work. Write down the skills and tasks that keep appearing. Look at what employers want someone to do, rather than collecting every tool or qualification mentioned once.

For an office support role, you might notice repeated requests for spreadsheet work. Look more closely. Are they asking for accurate data entry, formulas, reporting or something more advanced? "Learn Excel" becomes a more useful goal when you know what you need to do with it.
If you're still choosing a direction, the [career-change guide](/insights/career-change-south-africa-before-you-leave) can help you research the work before you pay to train for it.

sections.heading: Read the course outline past the headline
body: Find out what you'll actually practise. Does the course include exercises? Will anyone give feedback? Are there assessments, or do you receive a certificate for watching the material?
Check the starting level too. A course described as "beginner-friendly" may still assume knowledge you don't have. Ask the provider what you should already know and whether there is a sample lesson.

Think about how you learn. If you're comfortable working independently, recorded lessons may suit you. If you often get stuck without someone to ask, support and feedback may matter more than having a large library of videos.
Also check the equipment and software requirements. A course that is technically available on your phone may still involve practical work that's difficult to complete without a computer.

sections.heading: Understand what the certificate means
body: A certificate of completion can show that you finished a course. A vendor certification may involve a separate assessment set by a software or technology provider. A registered qualification or part-qualification has its own formal status. These are different things, even when the marketing makes them sound similar.

If a provider claims a programme leads to a registered qualification, ask for its exact name and SAQA ID, then check the [SAQA qualification register](https://regqs.saqa.org.za/). SAQA is the South African Qualifications Authority. Check the provider's authorisation to offer that particular qualification with the quality council responsible for it as well: the QCTO for occupational qualifications, the CHE for higher education qualifications or Umalusi for school and further education qualifications.

Don't assume every course offered by an accredited institution has the same status. SAQA's [guidance on quality qualifications](https://www.saqa.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Quality-Qualifications.pdf) explains why the particular qualification and provider need checking.

A short course can still teach a useful practical skill without being a registered qualification. The question is whether it meets your purpose. If a job requires a particular professional qualification, a general short course won't automatically meet that requirement.

sections.heading: Add up the full cost
body: Look beyond the advertised fee. Is the assessment included? Will you pay separately for the certificate, software, textbooks or a retake? How long will you have access to the material?

Data and transport count too. So does the time you can realistically give it. A course that needs ten hours each week will be difficult if you have two hours available after work and family responsibilities.

Read the cancellation and refund terms before paying. If the provider promises employment, ask exactly what that means and request the conditions in writing. Help with applications and a guaranteed job are very different commitments.

You can use the [free learning resource guide](/insights/free-sa-learning-resources-2026) as a starting list, but check the provider's current terms. Free access, certificates and funding offers can change.

sections.heading: Decide what you'll be able to show
body: Imagine an interviewer asking, "What did you learn, and where have you used it?" Plan for that answer before you start the course.

For a spreadsheet course, you could build a simple stock tracker with fictional data. Check that entries are consistent, create a summary and explain how someone would use it. For a writing course, you might produce a short set of instructions and ask someone to test whether they can follow them.
Label practice work honestly. Don't describe a fictional project as paid client work. Keep employer and customer information out of it unless you have the appropriate permission.

A finished piece of work gives you something concrete to discuss. You can explain where you struggled, what you corrected and what you'd still like to learn. That is more informative than listing a course title and hoping the employer fills in the rest.

sections.heading: Compare two options on one page
body: Before deciding, write down the following for each course:

items: The task I want to learn to do.
The lessons and exercises that teach that task.
The feedback or support available when I get stuck.
The certificate or qualification awarded, and what I've verified about it.
The total cost and the hours I can give it each week.
The piece of work I expect to finish.

body: You may find that a free introductory course is enough for your next step. You may find that paying for feedback or a recognised assessment makes sense. Choose on the basis of the gap you're trying to close, rather than the size of the discount.

sections.heading: What if you've already collected several certificates?
body: You don't need to dismiss the learning you've done. Go back to one course and ask how you can use it.
Could you complete a practice project, apply the skill in an agreed task at work or explain it clearly enough to help someone else? You might need more practice before you need another course.

If you're unsure which skill would help your next move, a [Career Clarity Session](/book/clarity) can help you connect your experience, target roles and learning choices. For today, find one advert for work you'd like to do. Circle one task you need to learn, and use that as the starting point for your course search.
